utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Monday, October 12th, 2009, and I greet everyone in this courtroom, first Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Praljak, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Pusic. I also welcome the Defence counsel, all members of the OTP, as well as everyone helping us. Let me first give the floor to our Registrar, who has a number of IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Two parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Vlado Sakic. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit IC1074, and the list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit IC1075. The CLSS internal memo, filed on the 25th of September, 2009, pursuant to the Trial Chamber's oral request dated 3rd of September, 2009, relating to Exhibit P09470, shall be given Exhibit IC1076. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Mr. Kovacic, I believe you wanted to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the court. Your Honour, with your leave, I would move for a request to have a number of pages for one's submissions extended. It is -- we are preparing a request for a reconsideration or, alternatively, the appeal against the decision regarding the admission of Jurcevic evidence. It is somehow very complicated work. In fact, we are analysing and contrasting documents of hundreds of pages and reviewing the decisions of the Trial Chamber, also the other Trial Chambers, in particular this Trial Chamber throughout the history of this trial. It is, in fact, an issue of first impression. Really, multiple submissions, and there are basically two submissions. One is reconsideration of -- for reconsideration of the decision, and the second one is for certificate to appeal. Alternatively, since there are basically two submissions and brought together for efficiency's sake, we would need an increase of the pages. We also include one question of -- we also include one question related to the decisions about expert reports concerning earlier expert reports like, for example, Dr. Donja and Dr. Mile because of the decisions it must be compared. Thus, altogether we are asking for maximum -- maximum of 4500 words. I do hope that we will not need all that. Probably it will be under this number, but definitely more than 4.000. We are now in the stage of final cleaning of the draft, but I think since there are at least two submissions in that paper and very extensive analysis of documents and the history of the case, we are asking you to permit us this extension. Thank you so much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has discussed this and is granting the request. The Praljak Defence can thus use 4.500 words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me give -- let me ask the Registrar to move to closed session or private session and drop the curtains, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're now in open session. Could you please give us your family name, first name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my name is Dragan Curcic. I was born on the 1st of September, 1965, in Zenica, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation, if you have one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not employed at present. I'm retired. I was a general -- lieutenant general by rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're a retired lieutenant general, but in which army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you have a military pension?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, have you already testified in court? If yes, could you tell us in which case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I testified in The Hague in the trial against Mladen Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down. Let me give you some details on what is about to occur. You have been called by the Praljak Defence, so you're a witness of Mr. Praljak, and you will be answering questions put to you by the counsel of General Praljak or maybe even by General Praljak, himself, if the questions are in his field of competence. Then the other Defence counsel representing the other accused will also, if they wish, put questions to you. The Prosecutor, on your right, will cross-examine you and will thus also put questions to you. And the four Judges on the Bench can intervene at any moment to ask you for specific details. Please try and be concise and specific when you answer. If you don't understand a question, just ask for the person putting the question to you to reformulate it. You are now a witness of the Court, a witness of justice, which means that if we're not finished with your testimony tomorrow, we'll continue tomorrow, but until tomorrow you are not supposed to contact the Praljak Defence team. Of course, if we can finish today, this won't be necessary. We break every hour and a half, but if at one point in time you don't feel well - sometimes a hearing is stressful and it's difficult to bear - so just raise your hand so we can have a break and so you can rest. I wanted to tell you all this to make sure that this hearing would run smoothly. I will now give the floor to Ms. Pinter, which I welcome again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, to you, too, and to everybody else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General, once again. In the proofing session for your testimony in court about the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993, we discussed your curriculum vitae as well. And in the set of documents that you have before you that, there's a page in yellow which says "CV," where we have your professional life listed. Now, I'm going to ask you whether the information on that sheet of paper is correct as we wrote them down.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes, this document is correct, the information there, and I gave you those facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, may we have a number, an IC number for that CV, for the General's CV, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have an IC number for the resume.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The witness resume, as indicated by the Defence counsel, shall be given Exhibit IC1077. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You told Judge Antonetti, when asked, that you are retired now, and that's the only correction actually made to your statement, is that right, the one you gave when we talked two years ago, when you gave us your statement? So the only difference is that now you are retired, and you were retired by the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, since you and I speak the same language, I'd like to ask you to pause, to help our interpreters, between question and answers. So please make a pause, and I'll try my best to do the same. We don't want to create any nightmares for our interpreters. Now, the document you have before you is 3D03759, 3759. I'm repeating that number for the record. That's the number of the document. It seems that the transcript isn't working for the Defence, but otherwise the central transcript is working. Is that the -- your document? Did you sign it, and did you state everything to the best of your knowledge truthfully there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, while we were preparing your testimony in court, you had a few observations to make with respect to the transcribed statement when you read it, and you indicated some mistakes that were made in the names. Now, take a look at the table that is also to be found in this set of documents, which lists the corrections you made. You asked that the name Ludvig Pavlovic be corrected and written properly, and the next name was Nijaz Batlak. The next correction was to the place called Urina Ravna, Atif Dudakovic was next, and Rasim Delic. Now, in this table, we list the page numbers where those corrections are to be found, so I'm now asking you whether those corrections were made as you requested when you noticed that there were certain mistakes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have an IC number, please, for that, for the corrections to the statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could we have an IC number for the corrections.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The corrected statement shall be given Exhibit IC1078. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, would you now take your statement up and go to page 3D43-0395. Those numbers are to be found in the right-hand corner, and it is 3D43-1221 for the English version. In that part of your statement, you're talking about how the barracks in Grabovina was taken control of, and you said that the guys who took part in the defence there had to learn that a war did not only mean fighting and combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, before moving into the content of the statement, I have a question. General, could you please shed some light on something that is written in your resume. I notice that from 1986 to 1988, you were an infantry specialist in Sarajevo, and then you jumped to 1992, where you were in the Croatian Army. I have two questions for you. What was your rank in the JNA in 1988, and what did you do from 1988 to 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, upon completion of the Military Academy, I was given the rank of second lieutenant, and I worked in Belgrade up until my departure to the Croatian Army, as a JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From 1988 to 1992, where were you stationed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in Belgrade, performing my duties until 1992, when I left to join the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Ms. Pinter, I apologise for interrupting, but I wanted to fill this gap.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, General, I asked you to look at 3D43-0395, and we were talking about the events of 1992, when the barracks in Capljina were liberated. And I paraphrased your words, where you described what that operation meant and how your men had to -- were confronted not only with the war but also death, and wounding, and prisoners. And you tell us, in that portion of your statement, that one of your soldiers slapped a JNA soldier who'd been captured and that the general shouted at that, and that you and Bozan said that nobody was allowed to touch anybody else. Now, what I want to ask you first is: What general did you mean when you say the general shouted at him? What general was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: I meant General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And who was Bozan?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: He was the late Bozan, commander of the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade, and previously he stood in for General Dajic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on that same page, you go on to say that this was necessary in order to set a model of behaviour to the men. So please turn to 3D406 now, please, or, rather, 430406 is the right number, and 3D43-0407. For the English translation, they are pages 3D431225 and 3D431226. So when you say that a commander sets the example to his soldiers about how they should behave, could you recount what you say there with respect to Busovaca of the 25th of January, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: The 25th of January, 1993, during the conflicts in Busovaca, my younger brother, who was in my unit, was killed along with two other soldiers, and one of them was my best friend. Some civilians had been taken prisoner and some soldiers were taken prisoner. And I allowed the women to have a smoke and light up a cigarette, and everybody wondered whether there'd be retaliation. They were all afraid of that. But I told the women that they could light up and that nobody was allowed to touch anybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, what was the significance of your behaviour? Were you sending a message of any kind? Was it a signal of any kind?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a signal to my men to tell them that they have to behave properly and as befits soldiers, and it was also a signal sent out to the civilians that nobody was allowed to touch them. And that should be the general model, that no civilians should be harmed if they were not a threat.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, the members of your particular battalion, your unit, were they educated and trained soldiers or were they just young men, fighters who had not been trained properly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: In my unit, I didn't have any educated soldiers, but they were trained because we had training exercises. But the fact is that most of them were young guys who were not married and who hadn't even done their military service in the JNA before the war, so that they came directly from secondary school into a war. So they were fighters or warriors more than properly-trained soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you turn to the next page, which is 3D43-0416, and in English it is 3D41-1230. Thank you. And here you say what you've just told us about members of your unit who went straight from school into military uniforms, without any military experience. And in order to be able to wield authority over such young men, it was necessary to be up at the front-line together with them and personally to put your life at risk. And you talk about two of your soldiers who did not want to go into action at Boksevica, which is autumn 1993. And then you go on to say that the general told you at the time that what you should aim for is that a subordinate comes to you and says that your life should be spared, which general are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to General Praljak, because during those operations he was at Urina Ravna, which was the most prominent position in that area, and the other soldiers were my company commanders who, after the killing of one commander, Bozan, wanted to protect my life and to keep me safe for our units and men. However, it wasn't -- he wasn't one to take the decisions. I made the decisions, myself, and of course I took part in everything. But we had this same example with General Praljak, when he went into operation directly with us. Sometimes you had to set the example.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What do you mean, the example was that he should go into action, into battle, or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, the example set was that I was at the head of my soldiers and the general stood at the head of all of us; not always, but frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, was that necessary?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, we could say that, militarily speaking, this is improper because the main commander should not be exposed and their life put at risk. But in view of the situation and the circumstances, and how we operated, it was a necessity.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now please look at page 3D43-0417, and in English that will be 3D43-1230. Here you describe the following, you said because sometimes when you come -- when you get there and you just burn out, and you're at some briefing, and he sees that you don't feel like anything because you're always exposed to rain and mud and dead soldiers and wounded, and then in the evening -- "and then in the evening, he would at some point assign tasks to us, which was worse for us than attacking a bunker. We also talk about the way to circumvent trains and so on, but the point was to change the atmosphere a bit." Now, General, whom are you talking about here? Who is "he"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: "He" is General Praljak, and this was in a situation where we had daily combat. There was bad weather. Lines were lost and fell, and we had to recapture them. So that in these briefings and these analytical meetings, when the general observed that we were really at our ends -- at our wit's ends, he would frequently -- he would sometimes even quote Tolstoy and he would assign tasks and talk about circumventing trains, and then we would just look at each other and start laughing. But this was for the purpose of, in fact, boosting up -- boosting our morale in order to fight the despondency.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, let's not go through the entire statement of yours, but in several places you mention certain events, and you mention the rank of general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Pinter, for interrupting. Witness, I would like you to give us a few examples of these tasks that you were assigned. I must confess it is not quite clear to me, what you are talking about. What kind of tasks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, well, that is precisely the point. The tasks were practically -- had no solution. It was a three-track approach. There were three tracks, there were cars on each of those tracks. So how do you manage to have all these cars running and not run into each other, not colliding? Or, for instance, imagine these young soldiers, who are not educated well, and then they would start laughing and say, Well, what are you talking about? The topics that they wanted to discuss were sports and things like that, but for the most part, we would always end up laughing. So this was more meant to -- the general really wanted to make us feel relaxed and to sort of try and forget the daily reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I understood that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me get back to Tolstoy, "War and Peace." Did General Praljak discuss peace, and did the soldiers then wonder what they were doing there? Did it make them laugh?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't say that the general discussed "War and Peace." I just used this by way of example, because he would start talking about Tolstoy for the benefit of these lads, because they didn't know who Tolstoy was. And, on the other hand, the general, if we discussed sports, then he would frequently move on to a topic where he was more comfortable with; for instance, literature and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I think I may lead you a bit. Now, the first tasks that you mentioned here that you were issued as assignments, they had nothing to do with the military and military assignments. They had more to do with maths and logical thinking; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Those tasks and what I mentioned just now was outside of the operations that were being planned and the conversations we had as soldiers. This was purely for the purpose of making us feel at ease, and because these lads were not really educated, he knew that, and he just wanted to bring these things up, and they would be surprised.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, let's not go through entire -- through your entire statement, but let me just ask you this: When you talk about the general, and you mention this general in various places, you just mention the rank, but you don't really use the name. Which general are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Would you now tell the Trial Chamber and everyone in the courtroom how it is that you are so certain that this is a reference to General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, I've read my statement, I've gone through it again, and I can say that that's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in closing, let me ask you this: From your resume and from your answer to the question by Judge Antonetti, I have to ask you this: What was your motivation to participate in the events in 1992 and 1993 in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but also in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, as a JNA member, to me it became obvious that this was not an army as it should have been, or at least what we thought it should be, so every individual tried to join their own ethnic group, their own nation. So when I deserted -- when I left the JNA, I could not stay in Bosnia and Herzegovina because the JNA was still present there, so I went to Croatia. But perhaps it's better to give you an example. If a Croat or a Bosniak remained in the JNA, then the Serbs would say that this was an honourable and a good man, whereas if a Serb joined the defence forces of Slovenia at the time, or Croatia, then they would proclaim him a traitor, so this was really not logical. And in this sense, there was this desire to help and defend my own people, and that was the reason that I was compelled or driven to leave the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So then you joined the defence of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I became a member of the 1st Volunteer Regiment, which was under the command of General Mate Sarlija, Daidza, whose base was in Vrbosko [phoen], in Baska Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned this in your statement, and you also said that you became a member of the HVO. What was your motivation to become a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Our unit was -- the main purpose of our unit was to provide weapons and to train those who wanted to fight in Bosnia, regardless of whether they were Croats or Bosniak. There were -- 40 per cent of our members were Bosniak. When the conflict broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, we insisted to go back because most people were originally from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Daidza, himself, was in favour of this, of us joining the fighting in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So we came to Bosnia and Herzegovina, but then we parted our ways with Daidza because he wanted to establish a large corps and we were not in favour of that, so we organised this unit, Ludvig Pavlovic, the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade, and it was in the ranks of this unit that we fought in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I don't know whether there's a translation issue, but I would like to repeat something you have said and which seems to me very important. You left the JNA and you joined the Croatian Army by becoming a member of the 1st Volunteers Regiment, commanded by General Daidza. You then add something else. You said that this unit had been set up to fight in Bosnia, so to speak. Is that what you actually said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said that it was established in order to arm and organise training for all those who were from Bosnia and Herzegovina and who wanted to fight in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've clarified, but there is still something which is unclear to me. The Republic of Croatia set up its army, of which this unit is a part. This unit is arming and organising all those people coming from Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then you added "and who wish to fight in Bosnia and Herzegovina." This is on line 7, page 19. So this is my question: At the level of the Republic of Croatia, did the authorities feel that the people there would be leaving for Bosnia and Herzegovina or had they set up a unit comprised of people originating from Bosnia and Herzegovina, but there was no telling that they might be going to Bosnia and Herzegovina one day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the 1st Volunteer Brigade -- Regiment, King Tomislav or Krajl Tomislav, was, for the most part, a unit where most people were from Bosnia and Herzegovina and also Croats from Bosnia, but often there were members of other units that were being formed in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They would frequently come and join us, and then they would be trained in Vrgorac, and after several days they would go back to the unit where they had come from. Whereas our members, the members of our units, were always within the establishment of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I need to correct the transcript. That's on page 19, line 22, the witness said "Croats and Bosniaks from Bosnia and Herzegovina." The word "Bosniak" did not -- is not in the transcript, and it is very important to know that this unit was made up of both these ethnicities. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, just one more question about your Ludvig Pavlovic unit. You said that it was established and that it was made up of members of this voluntary regiment; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Later on in the course of 1993, did you expel any member of your unit from the unit because that person was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Were members of your units who were Muslims, Bosniaks, were they able to remain in your unit in the course of 1993, in June, July, August, and September?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I have no further questions, and I just move -- thank you. That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have a follow-up question for you. We understand that this volunteers unit comprised both Croats and Muslims. These two groups came from Bosnia and Herzegovina. When you joined the HVO, were you told that you needed to go and join the HVO or was this a personal decision of yours, i.e., to join the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that was the decision of all of us who were originally from Bosnia and Herzegovina. We wanted to return and take part in the fighting in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and at this time in Croatia it was already a truce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among those who decided to go back to Bosnia and Herzegovina, were there any Muslims? In other words, were there any Muslim comrades of yours who said, We should all go back together to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there were. We all went back together. After a while, some of our members, both Croats and Bosniaks, went to Posavina because there was fierce fighting there. A group of our members, composed of both Bosniaks and Muslims, went to Sarajevo and then onward towards Gorazde, and about -- whereas about 100 or so of us remained in the area of Herzegovina, and there were Bosniaks and Croats in that complement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did any Muslims stay in Croatia and who remained cadre in the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All those who enjoyed the status in the Croatian Army retained their status as individuals. But after a while, the King Tomislav or Krajl Tomislav unit ceased to exist, so that all of its members moved to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answer. Let me take the case of a Bosnian who leaves Bosnia-Herzegovina to join this volunteers unit. He then decides to remain in Croatia. What became of him, since you have just told us that the entire regiment went to Bosnia-Herzegovina? What happened to this Bosnian, then, if he doesn't want to join the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, he would not have to join the HVO. He could stay in any unit of the Croatian Army. But all our members crossed over, regardless of whether they were Croats or Bosniaks or Muslims at the time. They all crossed over to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we fought together throughout this period, all, up until the conflict broke out between Bosniaks and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question. Did some return to Bosnia and Herzegovina with you and said that they wanted to join the ABiH or not? They didn't want to join the HVO, but the ABiH? Were there any such cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were many such cases later on. But when we had just arrived, there wasn't a single one like that because at that time we cooperated with the BH Army units and it didn't matter who was where if we were fighting a common enemy. But later on, when the conflicts began, most of the Bosniaks crossed over and joined the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, you were on your feet. Did you wish to say something?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thought that the interpretation might have misled the witness, but, no, the witness answered properly. And your question was if somebody from Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, I see that as our witness is a general, he understood what you meant and, of course, answered you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have one question for you. When you were in Croatia and a member of the volunteers unit, did you get paid? And if you did get paid, which ministry paid your salary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Ministry of the Republic of Croatia paid our salaries, but I think we only actually received one salary before we went to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When you went to Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you get paid or not at all? And if you did get paid, who paid you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the members of our unit who had a contract with the Republic of Croatia continued to receive salaries from the Republic of Croatia, and those who didn't have a contract would receive salaries from the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, when you commanded the professional unit of the HVO, Ludvig Pavlovic, who commanded the operational area then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there were several commanders of the operations zone. If you're thinking about South-East Herzegovina, where I was in Capljina, then -- then the commander was Drago Poljak, a colonel, and then there was Miljenko Lasic, who was a brigadier, and there was Nedjeljko Obradovic as well. So there were several commanders in that zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I understood, you took part in some fighting in the area of Novi Travnik, Busovaca, Boksevica, Prozor, and Mostar. You took part in a number of fightings [as interpreted] in this area. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to know this: When you were fighting - please listen carefully to my question, which is an essential question - did you have the feeling that the military operation was controlled and remotely controlled from Zagreb or you were part of a military operation which was, in essence, local, and you could, as well as the commander of the operational area, do as you wished, according to your own free will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think I've understood you. If the first question is whether I had the impression that there were -- the operations were led from Zagreb, then the answer is no. If it is did I take part in all these operations, the ones that were listed, I've already confirmed that I did take part in them and that I applied permitted methods used in armies in order to achieve my assignments and tasks. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood you correctly, under oath you are saying that as a commander of this professional unit called Ludvig Pavlovic, you never conducted a military operation under the control of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I conducted operations and orders I received from the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council. Now, the HVO Main Staff could re-subordinate me to a military district or operations zone to carry out assignments there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me get back to a final question which is also crucial. Your unit took part in the military operations in Mostar on the 9th of May; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a very accurate way, can you tell me at exactly what time you were asked to come and reinforce the military operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it would -- the most correct -- the exact time that I could say would be 4.00. That would be the closest. But I can't say exactly, but 4.00 a.m., basically. That would be the nearest time that I could give you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4.00 in the morning on the 9th of May. What happened at 4.00 in the morning on the 9th of May? Were you sleeping? How did things happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was sleeping, Your Honour. And I was woken up with the duty officer, and he told me that the unit had been called urgently to go to Mostar and that members of the BH Army were provoking the HVO and shooting at its soldiers. So with my intervention group, and we were able proceed in jeeps, we set out towards Mostar; across Citluk, however, because it was said that we wouldn't be able to pass through Mahala or the centre, and we reached Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what you are saying is essential. Either you are telling the truth or you are lying. There's nothing in between the two. Either you are telling the truth or you are lying. Let me remind you that you are here under oath. Can you tell me whether before 4.00 in the morning on the 9th of May, there was a plan to attack Mostar, or you only discovered all this when the duty officer woke you up at 4.00 in the morning to tell you to go to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't know about a plan of attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had there been a plan to attack by the HVO, would your unit have been preparing to launch this plan? I'm saying had there been such a plan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, had there been a plan, we would have to go and reconnoiter, do reconnaissance work, to establish this because we didn't know Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At 4.00 in the morning, you were sleeping. Where were your soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everybody got woken up in order to get up and go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, everybody had to be woken up, and then the jeeps and small cars set out. We set out first, and the other part of the unit followed us with the heavy-duty trucks, when they were ready to go and had loaded everything that needed to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you absolutely sure about the time, 4.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've given you the approximate time, the closest I could get to it, so I think it was thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did the duty officer have a log-book where he wrote the incoming orders or the incoming calls?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why didn't he have a log-book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it would be logical for him to have that, but we still were not an organised army in that sense, not sufficiently organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Pinter, you said you had no questions left. Does this mean that General Praljak has a question or does this mean that the examination-in-chief is over?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we've all finished, although I'm just getting a signal from the general that he has one more question. This has cropped up in the meantime. But the plan was to complete the cross-examination [as interpreted] with me, but now I see that the general does, indeed, have a question. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, General Curcic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Just two questions for you. The first is this, if you can remember: At what time did you, the first team from Capljina, enter Mostar? What time was it? The distance from Capljina to Mostar, the time it took for you to prepare, in your opinion, what was the time when you arrived, when the first people entered Mostar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: It was about 6.30, 7.00, 6.30 or 7.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And what about the bulk of the unit after you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: The men arriving after us, that was half an hour to 45 minutes later on, or an hour later, depending on where the trucks were with the three-barrelled guns and Bofors.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. And now my second question on the same subject. Had you received a plan of any kind, a plan of attack, beforehand to conduct reconnaissance work or any other preparations that would normally be undertaken before an attack like that on Mostar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: No, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, General, during the war did we, on a regular basis, have discussions and send men -- well, did I do all this, myself? Did I talk to them about how they should go to war and fight?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did, in your official capacity, and privately too. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me ask all the other Defence teams whether they have any questions. For once, we have some time in front of us. D1.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prlic Defence has no questions for this witness, and we place our time at the Court's disposal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Stojic Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Stojic Defence will have some questions, but according to our internal order the first Defence team to take the floor will be my colleague, Ms. Vesna Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For General Petkovic, Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you and everybody else in the courtroom, and good afternoon to you, too, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, the Trial Chamber and everybody else in the courtroom -- well, I'd like to inform them of our mutual relations, so tell us, did we have a meeting yesterday during the proofing session for today's testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That was the first time we had ever met; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, did I inform you briefly about the topics I'd be discussing with you which are important for the Petkovic Defence case, and did I say that I would be questioning you on those topics?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But before I go on with my questions, I'd like to ask you something about your response to Judge Antonetti's question, and that respond was recorded on page 26, lines 1 and 2. When Judge Antonetti asked you about the arrival in Mostar, and when he asked you whether you knew of the existence of any plan of attack on Mostar, your answer was the following: [In English] "I didn't know about a plan of attack." [Interpretation] Now, from that answer of yours, one could conclude that a plan of attack existed but that you knew nothing about that. Is that what you meant to say, or did you fail to express yourself properly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, the latter. What I wanted to say was that I knew of no plan of attack on Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, as a professional soldier and on the basis of your experience, when it comes to strategic military goals and the beginning and end of a war, as a rule is it the military commanders who make the decisions or is it the competent civilian authorities, the president, the president of the parliament, all the parliament, or whoever, depending on the setup of each state?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: The strategy of each state is made by the leadership of that state. The soldiers put into practice the tasks and assignments they are given and try to adhere to all the conventions on war law.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, General, that for you, as a professional soldier, it doesn't matter who is in power, whether it's the social Democrats or liberals, for example, and are you ready to fulfill your military assignments conscientiously and responsibly, regardless of which political party is in power?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, that should be the rule, madam, especially since a soldier has his commander, and soldiers have to listen to orders from their commander, unless this collides with human rights conventions and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, during the time you spent on the Bosnia-Herzegovina front, did you ever receive an order to do something which would be punishable under the law or were you asked to commit any crime?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In your statement, General, you speak about your unit, the Ludvig Pavlovic unit, as a special-purpose unit. Can you briefly tell us what these special-purpose units were and what their task was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: If you mean in general, what special units or special-purpose units mean, they are the units that are there to carry out the most difficult combat tasks, or diversions or whatever, and in the Croatian Defence Council they were units who were better trained, better equipped, and those who had a permanent setup of manpower.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, those units, did they act throughout the territory of Herceg-Bosna or were they linked exclusively to one municipality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: The professional units were of the manoeuvre type, which means that they could be deployed throughout the territory where combat was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And tell us about territorial units. What is their feature and what are the tasks of territorial units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, they defended the areas in their own municipality, or the neighbouring municipalities if there was no fighting in their own municipality, but their manpower, when they were on duty, they would carry out those military duties, but once they returned from the field they would do their ordinary work and jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, is the area where these territorial units acted or where they were active, was this the area where the line of conflict with the enemy was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the Siroki Brijeg Brigade of the HVO, in view of the fact that there was no fighting and no combat activities in Siroki Brijeg and that it did not -- that it was not in the bordering territories where there was fighting going on, what would their combat activities be of the Siroki Brijeg Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: The Siroki Brijeg Brigade was active in the territories of the municipalities that needed assistance, such as Capljina, Mostar, and that area, and sometimes they would also assist in Rama.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, the commander of the Siroki Brijeg Brigade, was he in any way active in the area of the Siroki Brijeg Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, no, he could just gather the men and then send them to the field. And then once they returned, they would -- he would take away the weapons from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please take a look -- I will show you a series of documents, and I would like to take a look at them. The documents discuss the number of professional soldiers of the HVO and the number -- and the soldiers in territorial units who had been mobilised. And I would like to remind the Trial Chamber that General Praljak, during his testimony on the 3rd of June, 2009, told us that there were about 1.000 professional soldiers and about 40.000 HVO soldiers. Now, General, would you take a look at the document P907, 907. Please look at page 3, the bottom of page 3. That is toward the end of item 3. This is a draft report prepared by Milivoj Petkovic, as the Chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, and it says there the total number of soldiers in HVO units is 45.000 men. The professional units have 855 members. Tell us, please, do these figures actually correspond to what you knew about the number of professional and territorial units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: I believe that the number mentioned for professional soldiers is correct, and I also believe that the total number for the HVO is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's take a look at how these things were in the course of eight months and whether the professional units were reinforced. Please take a look at document P4389. That's the next document we want to show. This is the report of the assistant Chief of the Main Staff, Mr. Ivica Primorac, who gives the total number of the special units, which does not significantly differ from the number that we saw for December 1992. Was this situation actually in accordance with what you know about the Ludvig Pavlovic unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, if I look at the Ludvig Pavlovic unit's situation, it is correct, and I assume that it's correct for all the other units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, now I would like to ask you about one particular unit, and this is the Convicts Battalion. Would you please take a look at the next document. That's 4D1356. We see this is an interview that -- on the 17th of March, in 2008, an interview of Mr. Ivan Andabak, who was the commander of the Convicts Battalion. The interview was published in "Globus." This is a political weekly that is published in Zagreb. And we can see the title, which says: "In the Convicts Battalion, Tuta was the ideologist and I was the one issuing orders. We were responsible to Susak and Boban alone." Now, please take a look at the last page of this interview. In the left column, and that is the only portion of the text that has been translated and the only thing that we want to take a look at now, the journalist poses the following question, I quote: "To whom were you responsible during the war in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina?" The answer is: "Exclusively to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, to Gojko Susak and to Mate Boban." Reporter's question: "And not to the minister of defence of Herceg-Bosna, Bruno Stojic, or to the commanders of the Staff, Milivoj Petkovic and Slobodan Praljak?" Answer: "We were responsible only to Susak and Boban." Tell me, General, did you know Mr. Ivan Andabak?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did Ivan Andabak, in your view, know who was the commander of the unit that he -- to whom the unit that he was in command of was responsible?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: In my view, he should know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you have any reason to suspect that Ivan Andabak would not speak the truth when giving statements of this sort?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please take a look now at the next document. That's 4D618. Here we have a schematic presentation of the HVO structure. This was used by General Milivoj Petkovic while he was testifying in a case before this Tribunal, in the case against Tihomir Blaskic. General, could you confirm or deny the statement that relates to your unit, Ludvig Pavlovic, that it was directly responsible to the Chief Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, just a minute. You are referring to the testimony of General Petkovic in the Blaskic case. When General Petkovic testified in this case, wasn't he granted protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, he did testify as a protected witness, but at the beginning of this case we submitted a request to the Trial Chamber to remove those measures because we wanted the Croatian public to know what the general testified to. But thank you for your warning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, could the supreme commander, Mate Boban, also issue direct orders to your unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now take a look at another document, P7419. I just want us to take a look at an excerpt. Listen to me. In the report of the Defence Department for the second half of 1993, the following is stated, and this is on page ending at ERN407 of the Croatian text. It says that in this period, there was a significant improvement in the structure of the armed forces, that the further development of the armed forces was conceptualised, and that there was a decision made on the establishment of professional units, and that all professional units which were not attached to the HVO HQ were abolished. In other words, all professional units which were not attached to the HVO headquarters were abolished. Now, General, when I connect this part of the report with the chart that was used by General Petkovic during his testimony, where the Convicts Battalion is presented as a unit which was not attached to the Main Staff, my conclusion would be that this was exactly that type of unit. Now, could you please comment on this? Is it true that there were, indeed, some units that were not subordinated to the Main Staff or are you unaware of what the structure of the other units was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the professional units? As far as I know, all the professional units that I know of were mentioned here. However, there were some ATGs, such as Tvrtko or the one in Livno. There was some special units who wanted to assume a certain name, maybe because of training or something, but these were the special units that were in the structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you about Busovaca, General, and during your direct examination today, you talked about the Busovaca area toward the end of January 1993. Please take a look at document 4D392. I would like you to take a look at the last paragraph of this document. This is a document from the Security Administration of the Supreme Command Staff of the BH forces in January 1993, and it reads as follows: "The Security Service of the 3rd Corps feel that the forces of the HVO in this area, in the event of a large-scale conflict, are capable of mounting a successful counter-attack to the HVO under the condition that the army cut off the road communications Busovaca-Povlaka [phoen]-Fojnica, Kiseljak-Fojnica, in Lugovi and Kacuni and also the road Busovaca-Vitez and Vitez-Travnik at Mecava, and also of the utmost importance of timely procurement of ammunition and grenades in this particular area." Now, General, could you please tell us about cutting off communications? Does that, in fact, mean the creation of enclaves?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this map now. That's 4D560, 4D560. This is a snap-shot of the territory of Central Bosnia in January 1993, and here we see that it says that the BH Army was conducting attacks in the area between Busovaca and Fojnica in order to cut off the communication lines between the two towns. Tell us, General, does this reflect what we've just read in the document that we saw a few moments ago on the screens before us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please take a look now at the next map. That's 4D561. This map is already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic. I'm not quite sure whether I understand what the map indicates. Does it indicate a plan that the HVO intelligence thinks the ABiH holds or does it indicate an actual attack?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Trechsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It is a question that I put to the witness. I think the witness should testify, but perhaps we have to explain because the witness perhaps didn't understand either.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thought that you were addressing your question to me, and that is the only reason that I began answering the question. But let the witness then tell you what was going on in January and whether what we discussed a few moments ago was just a plan or actual events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the basis of the paragraph based on the assessment of the BH Army about the communications that they were supposed to cut off, then what is shown on this map actually represents this main communication that actually cuts Bosnia into two parts, into Kiseljak and Vitez areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, that is the X that is here all blue. And then there is a red flash from the Kakanj area towards a bit north of Fojnica, and is that -- is that where the fighting actually went on or is it where it was feared that an attack might be carried, feared or prognosticised, analysed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to this, one would -- this would suggest that the army command was planning to cut off the territories that were under the control of the HVO along the areas where this arrow is, and this is what actually did happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So you're saying two things. First, you say this arrow indicates the plan, and, second, you say that there was actually an attack following this plan. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was not there when this was going on. But according to the plan within the 3rd Corps, and looking at this map, this is a good military plan. And as it turned out later on, the plan was actually implemented in this manner, because this blue areas, that were under control of the Croats, were actually cut off by the army. But I cannot really ascertain this because I was not a direct participant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, that's fine. That's a good answer, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Witness, looking at that arrow that Judge Trechsel asked you about, in that general area, is that where Kacuni are to be found?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, please, around that place and in that area, is that where there was fighting at the end of January 1993, which you refer to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: I fought on the other side. I wasn't in Kacuni, so I can't tell you anything about Kacuni. I was in other places.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But in your statement, you mention Busovaca and the area around Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Busovaca and at Busovacke Staje, but I was not in Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now, in the English version of your statement, it is on 3D43-0405. That is the part of the statement in English where we deal with this. Now let's look at 4D561. It's a map again, and it's already an exhibit. On this map, we can see that the BH Army managed to cut the Busovaca-Fojnica communication line, and this gave rise to the Croatian enclaves. Now, this depiction of Central Bosnia, does it correspond to what the situation was like on the ground, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I was looking at the two maps, and we see that in April the HVO is surrounded in Fojnica, Kiseljak, and another place. But looking at the first map in January, I see an axis Zenica-Travnik-Vitez-Novi Travnik. So why is it that the ABiH didn't close off this axis, because if it had done so, it would have totally surrounded the HVO? Why didn't they achieve this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, probably they weren't able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They weren't able to achieve this because of the reaction of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most probably, that would have been it, or because they didn't have the strength and power to do so, but it would have been logical for them to cut off the axis, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it would have been logical. Travnik was occupied by the ABiH, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did they control the road from Travnik to Vitez, thanks to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not the entire route. I don't know all the details, but it didn't control the whole road. Up to Dolac, at Lasva, somewhere around there, but the communication line from Novi Travnik to Vitez was free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not a military expert. I could have asked this question to an independent expert. But you are a general, so you might answer me. When we see those two maps, the one from January and the other one in April, could you tell us whether it doesn't look, military-wise, that the HVO was in great difficulty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Witness, a short while ago, on answering a question by the President, you said that Travnik was in ABiH hands. On the map, it is blue, so that looks rather as it was in the hand of the HVO. I hope I didn't misunderstand something. Travnik was in the hands of the HVO; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Presiding Judge said that Travnik had been taken control of by the BH Army and that the BH Army controlled the communication lines, but I said that I thought that they controlled the communication line only in part. Yes, the BH Army did take control of Travnik. I'm not sure during what period, but, anyway, they narrowed down this blue space here. Now, it was the Presiding Judge who referred to them taking control of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let's just clarify this. This map refers to the March-April period, and Judge Antonetti's question referred to June. So we're now going to look at maps which are going to tell us what the development of events was towards the end of the year, and we'll see how the blue territory diminishes. But I think that this is the time for the break. Right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was very much involved in the maps and I forgot all about the break. We shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. The Trial Chamber would like to specify, since this was not mentioned before, that as far as protective measures are concerned, the Trial Chamber has noted that the witness did not wish to be granted protective measures during his testimony in this case, and the Trial Chamber has also noted that the witness has specified that he did not wish to have those protective measures which he had been granted in the previous case. It's now on the transcript and is extremely precise. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's stay with the map we have on our screens for the time being, although I'll be calling up two more maps in that series. I'm afraid they haven't been prepared for the Trial Chamber or anybody else in the courtroom because I didn't intend to deal with them. But since the question of Travnik has cropped up, let's look at the next document, which is 4D562. It's a map which shows the situation on this same area in June 1993. On this map, General, we can see the axes of attack by the BH Army, and we see that the BH Army was active along the Travnik area, and then we have some other areas of conflict. But let's stay with Travnik for the moment and look at the next document, which is 4D563, which shows the situation on that same territory in July 1993. And here we see, General, that the BH Army has taken control of Travnik, that only a small part of the Novi Travnik municipality was under the control of the Croatian authorities. And can you tell us, if you know, General, whether that was how it actually was; that is to say, that in June 1993, Travnik fell and was taken control of by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, on this map, we see Bugojno as well. Do you have any knowledge about Bugojno, that in July that came under the complete control of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know exactly when, but I do know that Bugojno fell into their hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. I'm now going to ask you about the topics I said we would be discussing. Tell us now, please, General, when you or somebody else who was authorised to do so decides to incarcerate his own soldier because that soldier had committed some infraction, or for any other reason, for that matter, does your soldier then lose the status of an HVO soldier or not, when he's incarcerated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: You mean when we punish him? No, only if it's a crime which is punishable with a prison sentence. But, no, they don't lose their status.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And if they are -- and if he is convicted of a crime, then he would be put in prison, serve a sentence for that crime; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, please, this rule about retaining your status of HVO soldier if a soldier is incarcerated, does that hold true for all HVO soldiers, regardless of their ethnicity; that is to say, for Croats and Bosniaks alike?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have any cases of imprisonment, but the rule would apply to all members of the HVO, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Now look at 4D1466, please. And that is a document which the competent authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it's from the Tomislav municipality, in the month of February this year, sent to my Defence team's offices on the status of HVO soldiers, and my questions about that, soldiers who were in some detention centre or who, for any reason, were in detention or were not allowed -- did not have freedom of movement. So let's look at that document together. I'm going to read out almost all of the document, and it says that the time spent in the HVO units is recognised as a length of service -- double lengths of service, in conformity with the government of the Federation, on the criteria, methods, and procedure of recognising time spent in the defence of BH, and that this is counted as years of service during peacetime, recognising time spent in defence, et cetera. And I'm going to quote the most important portion of that document now: "Also for military conscripts who were in detention, prison, detention centre, or assembly centres or camps, regardless of the time spent, that time is also recognised as time spent in a military unit and, as such, is recorded as special length of service for retirement. If the official records do not match, then the client may request an administrative legal procedure to be initiated with the purpose of identifying the exact time spent in detention pursuant to a Red Cross certificate, military police or military unit records from the archives, or a statement made by the commander of the respective military unit."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Something went wrong probably in the translation. If you look at page 45, line 23, you read at the end the words "regardless of the time spent," but the text you have read says "regardless of the cause," "of the cause" or "duration," and I think "the cause" is of importance.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In the Croatian text, it is "on any basis" or "regardless of the cause."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the translation of the document is correct, so even if it is not correct in the transcript, you have the translated document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, what we've just read out, in your opinion, does it correspond to what you told us earlier on, that each and every one of your soldiers, if they are in detention, in prison and so on, remains an HVO soldier, and that the time spent in detention is counted as double time for years of service, just like if he was on the front; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, let's -- may we move into private session for a few moments, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, may we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, you mention in your statement the events on the Dubrava Plateau in mid-July 1993, the sabotage operations by the BH Army, and that as a result of these sabotage operations, the security of the Gubavica barracks was in jeopardy. And this portion is in your statement on the Croatian page 3D43-0423, 43-0423, and in English this would be on page 3D43-1233. General, I would like you to comment on a document that I would like to show you now. This is document 4D14 -- 1042, 1042. Yes, that's right now. This is a document, information, drafted by the deputy head of Military Intelligence Service of the Main Staff of the HVO. It was drafted on the 13th of July, 1993, and it was drafted pursuant to a conversation with a member of the BH Army whose name was Mustafa Beso, who was -- who said, among other things, the following: On the 12th of July, 1993, according to the words of the said individual, a meeting was held on Gubavica where members of the army were assigned with the tasks that were read out by Alija Djulic, who was the commander of the unit comprising of approximately 70 soldiers chosen from local people. The meeting was attended by about 50 soldiers who were assigned precise tasks, conquering the barracks on Gubavica. We think that the tasks were assigned to the Muslims in a similar scenario as in Bijelo Polje. General, could you please tell us what this remark relates to, the scenario as in Bijelo Polje?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a barrack of the HVO in Bijelo Polje that was taken or captured by the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was that because they were members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Further on, it is said that there were groups of soldiers of the BH Army who were assigned with the task of clearing up or cleansing the terrain and merging with a group, and the following place names are mentioned; the Dubrava area, the area Oplicici, Pocitelj, Tasovcici, Hotnja village. And then it says that they altogether were supposed to get reinforcement of some 700 soldiers, approximately, and that they were to head towards Stolac and Capljina, with the aim of obtaining full control over the Dubravska Plateau. My question, General, does this description of events actually correspond to what you knew when you were on the ground?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: I participated in this fighting personally, and I can confirm many of these things because I directly experienced them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, was there any other special unit that helped on that day to lift the blockade of the Gubavica barrack that is mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, I will tell you the first thing that comes to mind. The communication between Capljina and Domanovici was mined, but before that I would like to tell Their Honours that the manner of alerting units or soldiers was done in the same way. We were called on the phone and told that the Dubrava Plateau had fallen, so what happened is some 30 soldiers of mine and I went out on the spot and the first thing that we experienced was we found this communication that had been mined. We left our vehicles there and continued on foot to the command post that had not been captured, and then we headed for the center of Domanovici and towards Gubavica. In the Rudnik area, we had -- we came into direct conflict with the BH Army, and I had three dead in that conflict. This operation by the BH Army was organised in a very good manner. We were taken completely by surprise, and I think the only reason that they did not succeed was that they did not receive reinforcement from Mostar. But as for the liberation of Gubavica, I wasn't there. Rather, it was the members of the Bruno Busic unit that were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for the explanation. And now, just briefly, a few questions about another topic. We can proceed from the document that's approximately in the middle of that bundle that you have. That's document P1896. This document was drafted on the 15th of April, 1993, and sent to you and the Bruno Busic Regiment. It was issued by the Chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, Milivoj Petkovic, ordering the raising of combat readiness because of the situation in the Konjic and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the second toponym.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the area of Konjic and Jablanica. The second place -- toponym is "Jablanica." Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, tell us, did you receive this order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, from item 4 of this order and from the entire order, the Chief of the Main Staff is ordering -- or announcing that he would order your departure to a certain destination or area; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you receive specific assignments from the Main Staff for specific areas or did it transpire differently, in fact?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff was authorised to send my unit to a location whereby I would be re-subordinated to the zone or operations area commander, and I would receive specific assignments from them because they knew what the problems there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
