utterances.text: General, tell us, please, in mid-April 1993, was your unit engaged in combat operations in the area of Sovici and Doljani?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I only have one or two more questions that relate to Mostar. When you arrived in Mostar, who issued your combat assignment to you? Who told you where to deploy your soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: The combat assignment was issued on behalf of the operations zone either by Mico Lasic or Slavko Puljic. I can't recall with certainty which of the two, but they were the ones who told us where we were to deploy when we arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General, that is all. I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For Mr. Curic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, we do have questions in cross-examination. Good afternoon, once again, to everybody in the courtroom. Let me just have the usher hand the documents 'round. As I said, good afternoon to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And good afternoon to you, Mr. Curcic. We've met, have we not, during our proofing session, and we know each other from before as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Curcic, several times today during your testimony, or, rather, during your testimony in the Naletilic trial, you said what you said on page 54, lines 26 today, too, 26 to 53 [as interpreted] and on page 25 -- let me start again with the page numbers. Page 54, line 26, to page 55, line 3, and page 25, lines 3 to 6. Well, you repeated what you have said many times before, and that is that you only took orders from the Main Staff and that you were re-subordinated to the person who was the chief person in the area, whether it was the operations zone or the commander of a group. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now, if you take up the Petkovic Defence binder, I'm going to ask you to take a look at two charts, or perhaps you can look at your screen. It will come up on your screen. The first document is 4D1356. It's the chart showing us the organisational structure of the HVO for the period of 1992 and 1993, which was -- no, I apologise. Could Ms. Alaburic help me out with the number. Obviously, I've given the wrong number. The chart there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: 4D00618, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we have it. It's come up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Curcic, you said today -- or, rather, you confirmed, when asked by my colleague, that this was what the structure was like for the professional units, as it says here, and you also said that you received orders from the Main Staff and that you could also receive orders from the supreme commander, who was Mr. Boban; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let's look at 1992. Who were the professional units there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: In 1992, the professional units which meant something were the Bruno Busic colony [as interpreted], the Vitezovi, the Ludvig Pavlovic Battalion and the Convicts Battalion, and the ATG called Baja Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was that the situation in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And what changed in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, the Convicts Battalion was split in two to form two units.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now let's take a look at another chart drawn up by the Prosecutor. It is P9324.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I'm still looking at the organisational chart that's on the screen. I don't know where it comes from, but my eyes are attracted to the Convicts Battalion. We see that it is directly attached to the supreme commander, Mate Boban, but your battalion is attached to the Main Staff. Can you certify the truth of this organisational chart, the truthfulness of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the professional units were responsible to the Main Staff, but according to what Ms. Alaburic said and extracted from the interview given by the commander of the Convicts Battalion, we saw that they were commanded by Mate Boban and Gojko Susak. Now, in my specific case, it was the Chief of the Main Staff who was my commander, and I can't confirm anything with respect to either of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On line 9, page 58, to my great surprise you are saying that he was -- they were getting orders from Mr. Susak. What does Mr. Susak have to do with -- in relation to this Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no, I didn't say Susak was, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I might be of assistance, the witness referred to the interview by Ivan Andabak in "Globus," and the question was to whom was the Convicts Battalion responsible in Croatia and to whom in Herceg-Bosna. And then Andabak's answer was in Croatia, to Susak, and in Herceg-Bosna, to Mate Boban. And now the witness has linked the two, and it would appear that Susak was there for Herceg-Bosna too, which it doesn't say in the interview. But if you look at the interview, you'll see for yourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, could you please tell us where this organisational chart comes from and who drafted it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can tell you that, Your Honour, and I think I said it, although I couldn't see how it was interpreted. This chart was used by General Milivoj Petkovic when he testified in the trial against Tihomir Blaskic before this Tribunal, and this organigram was compiled by Milivoj Petkovic, himself. He was given questions in advance, and he knew that he would be testifying about HVO structure, so he wanted, in the simplest way possible, to show the territorial units and the special-purpose units in this way. So we're going to use this chart in our case and when we come to examine General Petkovic as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I shall also use it when I'll be putting questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the witness to look at document P9324, which is in that pink binder. It is the Stojic Defence binder, and I think it is the second document. It's a schematic compiled by the Prosecutor, and it was a chart used in another trial. But that doesn't matter, as far as our proceedings are concerned. May we look at the first page of that, please. That's right, that's the first page. And I'm going to ask the witness to take a look at that first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Curcic, it says here "Supreme Commander." Then we have the Defence Department and the Main Staff down that line, and then you see units for special assignments and professional units to the right. Now, according to this chart, were you in the blue area, where it says "Special-purpose and professional units"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Curcic, since you are in this chart and since there's a direct line between the Defence Department and this professional units section, and you were the commander of one of those professional units, can you tell us what your links were throughout the whole period, when you became commander or a fighter of this unit to the end, what were your connections with the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: We communicated with the Defence Department through the Main Staff. The Main Staff was in charge of us operatively, and the ministry dealt with logistics and other matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just to be precise, did you receive a single order from the head of the Defence Department for operational activity, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Now we're going to move on, Mr. Curcic, to another area, and that will be the last area that I want to examine you on. In your statement, on page 3D -- I'm referring to the Croatian text, 3D43-0409, and in English it is page 9 or 3D43-1227, is it -- do you find it difficult to locate that? But you can rely on my quotation of it. Anyway, you were speaking about Operation Bura, and I'd like to remind you what you said about that particular operation. You said that it took place in November 1992, and there were also attempts to liberate Podvelezje and the entire area between Mostar and Dubravska Visoravan -- Dubravska Visoravan so that "our unit had the hardest task, that of climbing up 690 metres, and that's when a big tragedy hit the unit." You go on to explain in your statement that Bozan Simonovic was killed during that operation, is that right, and then you go on to say that some goals were not realised: "We wanted to liberate the area entirely and force them out towards Hrgud and to Podvelezje, and our losses were substantial." Now, you've already mentioned the death of Mr. Bozan Simonovic. Now, I'd like to ask you to explain to Their Honours what Operation Bura was and how long it was prepared.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Operation Bura or Tempest is the second major operation after the crossing of the Neretva River by the HVO. All the effectives of the HVO were joint units together with the Bosniaks - the Bosniaks took part - and they prepared themselves for this liberational operation by which the Army of Republika Srpska was supposed to be forced out from Hrgud and Podvelezje and Stjepan Kriz and the surrounding areas of Stolac so as to make it impossible for them to shell Capljina, Mostar, and so on. The operation was a good idea, but we did not have the necessary materiel and effectives to put this operation into effect completely, and the tragic event with Bozan was a result because he was a legend during his lifetime, everybody respected him, and then we went on the defensive. But it was an operation which was designed to prevent further shelling of towns along the Neretva River valley by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, can you tell the Trial Chamber -- and you have already told us the parts of the territory and places where Operation Bura was designed to be effective. Could you explain to Their Honours what the length of this line was and from where the Army of Republika Srpska was supposed to be repulsed, the length of the front-line, in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, the environs of the town of Mostar, its eastern reaches, ending up with Mount Zegulja, which was west of Stolac, and according to my calculations and according to how the line was being held, it was a line of a distance of 70 kilometres. It was 70 kilometres' long.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, you said that in this operation, all the most important forces took part, both of the HVO and the BH Army forces at the time; that is to say, they acted jointly. Now, can you tell us which those units did take part in the operation? Which were they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: All the professional units of the Croatian Defence Council, Ludvig Pavlovic, Bruno Busic, the Convicts Battalion, and even the Vitezovi from Vitez were brought in to take part in the operation, and, of course, the 1st Herzegovina Brigade from Capljina, the Mostar Brigade, the Bosniak 1st Brigade. I can't list them all now, but, anyway, anything that was professional and all the capable men and units were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, how long did the preparations for this operation last?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: The preparations went on for a long time, and the operation was deferred several times due to a lack of manpower and also because there was a high concentration of Serb soldiers. So we prolonged the start of the operation for a long time, which meant that preparations were lengthy as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did you, perhaps -- in October in 1992, were you in Prozor at the end of October?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, these units which you listed, during that time did they conduct preparations for Operation Bura at the end of October and the beginning of November?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, all the units who were planned for the attack underwent preparations. I can tell you about my particular unit, if you like, but I can't speak for the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now let's take a look at two documents, the first of which is the one that comes after the chart, and it is 2D3057. Just tell me when you've found it. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, this is an order from the Chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, Mr. Milivoj Petkovic, dated the 6th of November, 1992, to the 1st Mostar Brigade, and he says: "With the objective of eliminating the direct attack on the city of Mostar and the wider area, and based on the previous agreement, I hereby command:" Point 1: "Prepare and execute offensive combat operations in the area of Podvelezje with the objective of taking the following features: Merdzan Glava, Sveta Gora, and Dobric." Now, I showed you this order during our proofing session. All I'm interested in now is this: Can you confirm, General, that this is precisely the order which referred to Operation Bura?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes. According to how this document is written, this is, to all intents and purposes, for Operation Bura.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And what about the 1st Mostar Brigade; can you tell us what kind of brigade that was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: I think it was a BH Army brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the next document. That's 3D3528.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I would like to look again at this order of General Petkovic preparing an offensive. There are five orders in this -- five points in this order. It's very specific, but when looking at it, I wonder the following: If HVO had attacked ABiH on May 9th, wouldn't there have been an order that would have been similar to this one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the order for the 9th, that's something I've never seen, and I had never seen this order, either, until Madam showed it to me. And when I say that I think that it is authentic is because it says here in the preamble "based on the previous agreement," so it would appear that they had already discussions about the issuance of orders to this brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you confirm that this order on the screen is an attack order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this order is identical to the ones we've seen before. It orders preparations for an offensive operation to be carried out, and it even contains things to the effect what should be carried out, and there is no feedback -- no follow-up information as what had been done or not, because based on a feedback report we would know whether something had been carried out or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: However, sir, in relation to this order and the consequences of Operation Bura, unfortunately, and I say "unfortunately," we will see that there was an operation, and I say "unfortunately" because there were dead and wounded soldiers. Could you now please take a look at document 3D3528. Have you found that? That's the next document. This is a report from the Medical Service, and it says "Bura" in parentheses, the HVO Medical Service of the Operation Zone Eastern Herzegovina, dated the 9th of April, 1992. Witness, can you confirm, because we see here in the first sentence it says "the plan for medical security for Operation Storm" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "For Action Bura," interpreter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- what -- why was the name Bura chosen? Do you know that in 1945, there had been another Operation Bura in the same region.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What year?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1945.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, sir. Your Honour, just to clarify something to make sure that there is no confusion, there are two different operations. In our language, these were Operation Storm and Operation Tempest. "Storm, "Aluja," that is a completely different term, a completely different term, and it's not Operation Bura or Tempest. "Bura" is a wind blowing from the sea toward the land mass, and "Storm" is something that can actually arise anywhere else, so these are two different terms. The Operation Storm is an operation from 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, when I'm asking a question, it's always a very specific one. General, in 1945 the Germans launched an Operation Bura in the region of Mostar, and in 1945 this word "bura" was actually used, so can you -- do you have any idea why this word "bura" is used so extensively?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born and lived in Zenica. I had not lived in Mostar or Herzegovina before the war, so I did not really know exactly the meaning of the word "bura" or that it related to wind, because we used different names for winds where I came from. I didn't know this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I had never heard of this operation in 1945. I apologise. It's probably my error. I was born after 1945, but I had never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So, Witness, have you found this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We said this was a report. Does this report relate to this operation, Operation Bura or Action Bura? It says in the first sentence that the plan for medical security for Action Bura was prepared on October 22nd, 1992, and to date it is being implemented in the field. Does this confirm, General, what you've already said, that this action had been prepared and planned for earlier and then delayed, and that it only actually came into effect in November?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please now take a look at page 3. In English, that's page 4. That's the Medical Service of the 7th Battalion from Blagaj, and we see here a report on the losses in the area, in the area of the 8th Battalion. Here we have a list of dead and wounded soldiers, and you told the Trial Chamber that HVO and BH Army units together participated in this operation. Now, can we see here -- we see the HVO units. We see the losses mentioned there, and we see that there were casualties, both Muslim and Croat. Could you please take a look at this list, and then, based on the names, could you tell us what your conclusion is as to what their ethnicity is? So the name of these people who were wounded in this operation. Just take a look at the first page and the list of names, and go under names 1, 2, 3.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Kemo Jugo, Bosniak; Sejo Gasdan, Bosniak; Nusret Batlak, Bosniak; Omer Hubanic [phoen] -- well, I'm saying all this based on their names, the usual names used by Bosniaks, Croats, and Serbs. Omer Hubanic, Muslim; Ibro -- Marinko Grbasa [phoen], Croat; Stanko Sesar, Croat; and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We will not discuss the spelling of the names in the transcript. But the first five names that you mentioned, these were the names under 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, and you said for them that they were Bosniak; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The individuals whose name you mentioned as possibly Croats are the individuals under 6 and 7 on this list; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We can see that at the end of the list, we have the names of two dead individuals, and we see that this entire list was compiled by the commander of the Medical Department of the 7th Brigade, Dr. Edin Obradovic. Can you judge, from his name, what nationality or what ethnicity Mr. Obradovic was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, judging by his name, I would say that he was a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We have another written report from the 1st and 7th Battalions, although it says here that they have not come in. For the 1st Battalion, it is stated that there was one dead soldier, and for the 7th, that there were 40 wounded and 5 dead soldiers. Now, please take a look at the next page, where the 1st Herzegovina Brigade is mentioned or, rather, the list of dead and wounded members of that brigade in Action Bura. The date is again the 9th of November. Would you please take a look at the wounded soldiers under 5 and 6. Do you know these men?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes. These were my soldiers. The third man -- the man under number 3 and under number 7, they were also my soldiers, Mate Nikolin [phoen] and Pavlic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell us, please, under 2 and 3, these two names that we find in this report, again based on their names, can we conclude that these were Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, please, on the last page, we have a list of dead troops, dead soldiers. We see the name of Mr. Bozan Simovic, the commander of your unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As far as you know, were there many casualties in the Army of Republika Srpska, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I -- we didn't get that information or those facts officially.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell us, on the basis of information that you had at your disposal, what was the number of casualties in your area or in your unit where you were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: In my unit, there were three wounded and one dead soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, thank you. Thank you, General, I have no further questions. And thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everyone has put their questions. The Prosecutor now has the floor for the cross-examination, Mr. Laws, unless you had rather we have the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm prepared to start now, if it suits the Court. Good afternoon to Your Honours and to everyone around the courtroom. Perhaps just a moment while my binders are given out. There are two binders. One contains the documents that I'll be using for cross-examination, and the other contains the transcript of the testimony of this witness in the previous proceedings that we've heard about. General Praljak is trying to attract the attention of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: If everybody has sight of a binder:

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Curcic. Is it right that in 1993, the Ludvig Pavlovic --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you -- the Ludvig Pavlovic brigade were based in Capljina; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: It's not the brigade, it's a battalion, but it was in Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction. Your battalion was based in Capljina and that's where the barracks were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Witness, please, a while ago we talked about a brigade called Francetic. Could you tell who Mr. Ludvig Pavlovic was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Ludvig Pavlovic was a man who was born in Vitina, near Ljubusko, and he was a Croatian emigre and was arrested by the Yugoslav authorities and put in prison by them for 20 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: He's a hero to Croats, isn't he? To some Croats, anyway?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. I was asking you about Capljina. Is it also correct that from the summer of 1993, you had an apartment in Capljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I want you to look with us, please, at a document in the binder I've just given you, P02608, which will give us, I think, the date of when you obtained that apartment. It's page 4 in the English. For you, Mr. Curcic, it's page 2, in the B/C/S, at the foot of the page. And if you look, in passing, at page 1, it's a letter that you're writing to Bruno Stojic, I think. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Let me just try and find the translation into Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Just like the other binder, we've got the English first and then there is the Croatian text immediately behind it. The English document is 11 pages' long, and then you'll come to a document in your own language. That's it. This is a document that you sent to the Defence Department, and we can see, on page 2 of the English, that it is addressed, amongst others, to Bruno Stojic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And for you, it's page 2, the second page of the document. At the foot of that page, you can see your name, "Dragan Curcic." Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And as I say, it's page 4 of the English. You appear to have obtained an apartment in Capljina certainly by the time of this letter, which is the 2nd of June of 1993. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And I don't really want to spend very much more time on that document, but you were keeping -- for reasons we perhaps don't need to go into, you were keeping the Ministry of Defence informed about who was having apartments from your battalion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, obviously this was produced pursuant to the request submitted by the ministry, and we are providing information on apartments that were temporarily assigned for use of our members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. So I want to see if I've got the picture right as of the summer of 1993. You would spend some of your time in Capljina when not deployed on the front-line with the Ludvig Pavlovic Battalion; would that also be right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not the entire battalion. Members of the battalion, if they had days off, they would go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes. It's probably a problem of translation. I'm talking about you. You would spend your time -- some of your time, when not fighting on the front-line, in Capljina, at your flat or at the barracks, but in Capljina, itself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I want to ask you, first of all, some questions about things that were happening in Capljina in the course of that summer. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You've been asked some questions already about an order that was given to detain Muslim males. We know that order was given on the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please, Mr. Laws. I have an ancillary question as compared to the questions you are putting, but to me this is an important question. The flat you have, which is 74 square metres, was a flat which was given to you because you seemingly were a refugee or somebody that had been expelled, and your previous place of residence was in Belgrade. I see that if I look at the address of this apartment, there was a previous tenant or owner -- or, rather, tenant in this flat, Tomislav Jovanovic, and I see that most of these flats had been occupied by Serbs. There are only Serb names on here. I note also, on looking at the document, that a commission had been set up, since this commission is also one of the addressees of this document. And I can also see that in this document that Mr. Pero Markovic from the Capljina municipality is also an interested party. Now, I want to put this question to you: This flat which was given to you, was it given to you because it was vacant because the Serbs had left, and was it a municipal commission that gave you this flat, or was it the army, the HVO in this particular instance, that requisitioned the flat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, the flat that was assigned to me was an apartment of a former JNA officer. The entire building, in which that flat was that was assigned to me, was a building where members of the JNA had lived before the war. As you know, we liberated the Capljina barrack, and even before its liberation all the Serbs had already crossed over to the other bank of the Neretva and left Capljina. So these apartments were abandoned, they were vacant, and the commission that was set up by the operations zone, they made a list of these apartments, and then we assigned them to those members who did not have their houses or homes or apartments in Capljina because they weren't from Capljina, they weren't living there. Also, apartments were assigned to all the members of the families of the dead soldiers. So let me again reiterate, most of these apartments were owned by Serbs, but they had left them, and as of this day -- nowadays they had all managed to recover these properties, and they resettled them, lived in them, or, through a court, they managed to recover their rights on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. We have an intervention in the transcript. On page 64, line 4, the sentence should end with the words "all the members of the soldiers who had been killed were assigned these apartments on a temporary basis." So this witness is testifying throughout this time about apartments being assigned on a temporary basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are right insofar as these flats were lived in by Serbs, but I would like to draw your attention to the fact that there was a flat which, prior to that time, had been occupied by Sakib Mahmuljin. Do you know who Sakib Mahmuljin is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is Sakib Mahmuljin, a general in the BH Army and a deputy minister of defence, and he was serving in Capljina before the war, in the JNA, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His flat was occupied because he had left or because this flat had been taken from him? There is a difference, of course. I'm sure you understand. That's why I picked this up, because I saw the name Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Sakib Mahmuljin was in Zenica at the time. He was a commander there, and he fought in Zenica, and the apartment was vacant. When he returned, he managed to recover it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You've been asked some questions today about an order that was given on the 30th of June of 1993 to arrest Muslim males of military age. Can I ask you this: Were you aware, at the time that that order was issued, that it was taking effect in the Capljina area?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that this is a bit confusing to the witness, because as far as I recall, there was no question asked of the witness; rather, my colleague actually read this out for the Trial Chamber. So I just want to make this clear so that the witness is not confused. The question was whether he was -- a reference was made that he was asked this question, but it wasn't asked of him, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to Mr. Kovacic for intervening, as always, to assist, but I strongly suspect that this general is capable of telling us if he's confused. And the question wasn't intended to confuse him. It was intended to elicit from him an answer to the question whether or not he knew, as it was being implemented, that an order of that kind had been issued. It's not a confusing question. If the general finds it so, he's, we respectfully submit, perfectly capable of telling us. So with your leave, I'm going to ask it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Were you aware --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I think I was probably misinterpreted. All I said to my colleague was -- I put to him the words that he had used in his question. He said to the witness, You were asked today about the 30th of June, 1993. In other words, he's putting to the witness something that is not correct. I have no objection to my dear colleague asking the witness about his knowledge about the 30th of June, but he cannot actually impute words that the witness had not used. He cannot impute things that are not true. So that is the gist, and that's the only thing that I object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws, Mr. Kovacic is right insofar as this date of the 30th of June has not been mentioned. However, questions were put to him on the fact that Muslims had been detained. Perhaps it was in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And I think you'll see, with respect, that the transcript shows my very first attempt to formulate that question included, in parenthesis, "we know the date to be the 30th of June." I don't think there's any dispute about that, and, I'm afraid, respectfully, I can't see why we're taking up very much time with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Mr. Curcic, on the 30th of June, an order was issued, and we can look at it together, if you wish, but an order was issued to detain Muslim males of military age. My question to you is this: Did you know about that order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Could you show it to me, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I certainly will. In the bundle that has been given to me, it's P03019. P03019, and it's a document dated the 30th of June. And the paragraph that you'll want to read is paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: I have read it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. As June came to an end, we've seen that order. As July began, were you aware or not that it was being acted upon, that that order was being obeyed in the Capljina area?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just an objection to this question, because from this order we can see that it never arrived in the HVO units in Capljina, but that it only arrived and was received by the 1st and 3rd Brigade in the operations zone, which is the Mostar area. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws, there's a mistake. It's not the 1st and 3rd Brigade, but the 2nd and 3rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Shall we, with respect, just take it relatively quickly and go to the next document that helps us with this, which is P03134, and we'll see whether or not it's been implemented in the Capljina area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you didn't answer the question. This document, well, had you been made aware of it, had you seen it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not this one, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, let's try and be a bit more specific, if we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Perhaps not that piece of paper, but were you aware that there was an order to arrest Muslim males of military age at the end of June? That's a yes-or-no answer, with respect, Mr. Curcic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it's very difficult to give a yes-or-no answer, but I can give you an answer. I personally took part in a disarmament -- in disarmament in a specific location, but we can deal with that when we come to it later, in the area around the village of Rotimlje. And it's not illogical to disarm someone if somebody trains that weapon against you. There are less losses that way. And I specifically haven't seen this order, but we did conduct a process of disarmament.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: We're going to have a little time together, you and I, Mr. Curcic, and with the greatest of respect, I haven't asked you anything about whether it's logical to disarm someone or whether it's a good idea. I just want to ask you if you knew about it, that's all, and I've asked you it a number of times now. Is your answer that, yes, you knew that Muslim males were being arrested as June came to an end and July began in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I acknowledge that I did that personally, so, yes, but I can't confirm this order because I've never seen it before, so I can't lie and say anything with respect to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: No one wants you to do that. Let's look at the next document that's going to help us with --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can we be very precise here, please? Mr. Laws used the term "Muslim males," which, in the order that we read out a moment ago, is not what it says. It says "HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnicity." That's the first point. And, secondly, the Muslim inhabitants who were military conscripts, so not defined as Muslim males.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: If I may reply to that, the order says women and children should be left in their houses and apartments. In my respectful submission, that leaves Muslim males as the target of this. So the Court is quite capable of reading all of these documents, themselves. My questions aren't in any way misrepresenting them, and I'd ask that we now try to make some progress. We have a way to go on this topic alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just a minute, Mr. Laws. A number of objections have already been raised about this document, and the Trial Chamber is fully informed of this. Maybe you were here in the courtroom at the time. On paragraph 8, for example, it says that "must be disarmed and isolated," the soldiers. It says "soldiers." It doesn't say "Muslim males," it says "soldiers." And then in the rest -- the rest of the paragraph deals with women and children and possibly also men who were not soldiers. We've already mentioned this at length a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: May I continue after the President here. Of course, here are a number of documents, and if we are looking at the document which was previously brought to our attention, that is, P03019, 3019, there on page 2, in paragraph 8, the second indented paragraph, it is there. We can read, and I quote: "In the places within the area of responsibility where there is a Muslim population, all military-capable Muslim men should be isolated. Women and children should be left in their houses and apartments." So, of course the -- and I would say that Muslim men -- "military-capable Muslim men," as an expression and category, has been mentioned here, and elsewhere as well, and it would be really very good if the Prosecutor could proceed with his cross-examination. Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm very grateful to Your Honour. Thank you. Can we look at the next document, P03134, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we should have the break. It's time for the break, and we will continue with document P03134 after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Just in case we've lost the thread at all, Mr. Curcic, I'm asking you about people being arrested in the Capljina area in the summer of 1993, and I'm going to ask you to look next at another document. I'm going to make it plain -- perhaps it will save some time. This has nothing to do with Mr. Petkovic, but let's have a look at what was happening in July, the 3rd of July, 1993. P03134. This document doesn't have the names of any of the accused upon it, and I hope we'll be able to look at it and just see what it tells us. It's page 2 of the document in the B/C/S, and it's page 3 of the English. In both documents, it's very close to the center of the page under the heading "Course of Significant Incidents." Can you see that, Mr. Curcic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you may need your microphone on, or two.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Would you just read to yourself the words that follow that heading, "Course of Significant Incidents," under the subheading "Incidents of Security Interest." Just read that paragraph to yourself, if you would. You need to read as far as "Neum municipality," and then you can stop.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: What's being spoken about there is the arrest of 1.820 people who have come from the municipalities of Capljina, Stolac, and Mostar. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Can I ask you the same question as I was asking you a little earlier? Were you aware of these large numbers of people being arrested, let's say, in Capljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You weren't aware of it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: For so many people?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, it's not really a question which is specific to the exact numbers. Were you aware that significant numbers -- lots of people were being arrested in Capljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: No, sir. I knew that people were being arrested, but I didn't know the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, it sounds like we may not be really disagreeing. You knew that people were being arrested, but you didn't know, what, the precise numbers, or you didn't know it was as many as 1.820; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I knew that some people had been arrested, but I said that I didn't know the number. And we also saw from the order earlier on, applying to the military-able men and members of the BH Army, that they were arrested in other areas, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes, there isn't any doubt about that, and people are arrested in wartime and in peace for all manner of things. But I'm asking you about this wave of arrests, and you know what I mean. You can answer the question, if you choose to. Were you aware that lots of people were being arrested all of a sudden in July?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: No, could he answer that question? It's not a difficult question. Could he answer and then could we hear --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just an objection to the way it was said, "all of a sudden in July," and I'd like my objection to be recorded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. I don't know if I need to reply to that or not. Can I do, so, because it might just help us. At page 3, it says "this work has already taken three days," the document is dated the 3rd of July. It happened all of a sudden, and I don't know if I can argue it any more forcefully than that. The document speaks for itself. I appreciate that people want to be very precise about things, but the reality is we're going to get there, however long it takes, in my submission. So may I, with the Court's leave, now move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Would you look, please, at P03940. I would ask you to look at that. I'm going to ask you to try my question that elicited the last objection. Were you aware that all of a sudden people were being arrested in large numbers in July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at this document. It's dated the following month, the 4th of August, 1993, and you have, I think, had a chance to look at it in the few seconds that have passed since you were shown it first. Is that right, you read it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And it tells -- it is an order that the Muslim population should be rounded up, that no attention should be paid to their age, that they should be taken to two collection centres in Pocitelj and in Sevac, Sevac Polje, that if they resist, then the soldiers arresting them should open fire, and the order is to be carried out as from the 5th of August; can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It relates to something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, how can you explain, militarily-wise, that number 2 -- in bullet point 2, it says: "Do not pay attention to age"? Let me take a theoretical example. Let's imagine that we have children, 10 -year-olds, 12-year-olds, 6-year-olds, and maybe even a 2-month-old baby, everyone will be arrested, everybody should be arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That shouldn't be the case, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not supposed to be that way. But when you look at the order, if I'm, you know, a soldier, a dumb soldier, I'm told not to pay attention to age, so I arrest everyone, if I read bullet point number 2 and obey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I did not write this order and, secondly, I wouldn't issue such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: No, but what I'm asking you is whether you knew that the events that are being ordered there were taking place; that's to say, the round-up of the wider Muslim population was taking place during that summer. Were you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you wish to say that I knew about each of these detentions. I personally took part in taking some people into custody, and I don't wish to avoid saying that, but I can't know about anything else. I had different activities to attend to and I couldn't follow all this. I knew that some people were being arrested, but I didn't know of the figures and I didn't know how. And as you can see, this order did not refer to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting for a moment that it refers to you. I'm asking you if you knew -- let's take specific examples. Did you know that women and children were being arrested?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Look at it like this: Whether women and children were arrested, well, probably there were certain arrests like that. I know that they did arrest the people who were military able and who wanted to change sides, to go from the HVO to the BH Army. That women and children were arrested, probably they were, but I wasn't in charge of those prisons, but I do believe that women and children were arrested too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Let me try and help you, please, Mr. Curcic. There isn't any doubt at all that women and children were arrested. There's no "probably" about it. The question is: Did you know about it? It's not a hard question. You've answered a totally different question, a question you'd rather have been asked, rather than the one that I did ask. Did you know that women and children were being arrested?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already answered that. I do believe that they were. I believe they were. I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: That is not an answer, and you know full well it is not an answer to the question. Do you know -- did you know that they were being arrested? To say "probably they were" is not an answer. We know they were. I'm asking you if in the summer of 1993 you knew or not.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, often if they took away the men, it would be illogical for them to leave behind the women and children in the villages. Other units could turn up. So I do believe that they did take away the women and children, not with the aim of incarcerating them, but to save them. Now, not all soldiers were under control, so these detentions and these arrests were not only done ex officio, in the line of duty, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness. I have the feeling that I have to recall your duties to you. You should answer the questions the way they are put to you. You have now persistently avoided to do that. You have said something else, and I cannot imagine that you did not understand the question which was so simple a question. Did you know about that time? Did you give a lot of explanations. You're not asked to give any explanation. The only question is whether you knew that this was happening at that time, and no "probably," "yes," and "perhaps logical," nothing of that kind. This is the way the Tribunal operates, and I would be grateful if you could conform to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I, personally, never saw it, but, yes, they were. But I, personally, didn't see it. That's why I kept saying "I do believe," "I'm sure," or whatever, but I never saw it. I never saw them take anyone, but there were cases like that, and you can't get away from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Whether you saw it or not, you knew full well, by August of 1993, that women were being not only arrested, but also mistreated; you knew it full well, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: No, but I do know that one of our members asked that at all costs they try to pull his mother out, because the encirclement that she lived in, there were many members -- former members of a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, you know the document that I'm about to show you. When did you last see the document that you've just referred to? When were you last -- when did you last sit with the document that you're about to talk about, in your hands, Mr. Curcic? You know the one I mean. When did you last see it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: It's like this: You're asking me, and you say that I must have known, that I certainly, of course, I knew when Klepic [as interpreted], who was with us, asked that his mother be protected and that she be allowed to leave or enabled to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: When did you last see the document that you and I both know we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's turn to it, then, shall we. P03991, a document written by you, Mr. Curcic, on the 6th of August of 1993. Do you want to read it out for us? It's addressed to the police station in Capljina, isn't it? Do you want to read it out for us so that we have it in the record?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Certainly. The subject says: "Request." "I address you with this request to exempt from maltreatment and from being taken away Ms. Fatima Klepo because her husband has contributed to our unit in many ways, and to enable her to move freely around the Capljina municipality, hoping this request will be positively answered. I thank you in advance," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Is it husband or son?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Her son," interpreter's correction, "Her son."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So you saw that document yesterday, and the line of cross-examination that I'm pursuing is absolutely no surprise to you, is it, Mr. Curcic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: No, sir, I do have this order. If you have it, I have it, too. Therefore, if you have received it, you must have received it through my archives. Do you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The way this is going to work just at the moment is I'm going to ask you some questions. All right? What did you mean when you said that you requested that Ms. Fatima Klepo be exempted from maltreatment and from being taken away? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Her son came with a request. He asked us to do that for her because he was one of our members, and many people who moved around at that time were out of control. And, of course, I would do the best for each of our fighters, and so on the basis of that, this request was written to the police station, asking them to protect Ms. Fatima Klepo in every respect and to enable her to move around freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Was her son called Senad Klepo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: One of her sons was Senad Klepo, and I don't remember the other one's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I just want to collect, if we may, on our way through one detail about Fatima Klepo. We're going to spend a little bit of time with this document, but let's just get some details. Senad was one of the gentlemen in your unit, and if we look together at a document much further on in the binder, P11066, we'll get his date of birth. P11066.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: This is a letter by one of your predecessors as commander of the Ludvig Pavlovic, and it records that Senad was born on the 1st of June of 1959?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: By August of 1993, if he was still alive, he would have been 34?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Which if we come back now to his mother, Fatima, in P03911, would mean that even if she had had her son when she was 18 years old, she'd be a woman in her 50s, wouldn't she?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know Mrs. Klepo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: But we can work out her age very approximately, as a minimum, that she's in her 50s, at least, to have a son of 34 in 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes. So the woman that you're writing about, who you're asking the Capljina police to ensure is exempted from being maltreated and being taken away, is a woman in her 50s, at least?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, according to those calculations, yes. I never met Mrs. Klepo. I did meet her sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Why would anyone be taking away from her home and/or maltreating a woman in her 50s?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, didn't you ask -- when you say one of her sons asked you to intervene, didn't you say, Well, what are you worried about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, people were worried. That's why they came with this request. They asked of us to try and protect them in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So you better tell us how you say this letter came about. A man comes to you and says he wants your help to protect his mother; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And you think that the best thing to do is to write to the Capljina police station and ask them to assist you in having her not taken away or mistreated; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, he literally asked for this mostly because of the maltreatment, because -- I don't know exactly where they lived, but I think that near where they lived, there were some members even of the HOS, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: They lived, it would appear, close enough to Capljina police station for you to think it worthwhile getting them enlisted to assist her; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I was trying to help my soldier. He came with this request. I never knew this woman, this lady, nor would I have written this letter had he not asked for it. I -- and I never checked with him what kind of problems she was having and what kind of maltreatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, we may come back to that in a moment. I'm going to suggest to you that this is a letter that is written by somebody who knows very well that women, to take this example, are being taken away from their homes and are being mistreated. That's what I'm going to suggest this letter tells us, first of all, and that state of knowledge, I'm going to suggest, was yours. You were living there and you knew it was happening, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what you're saying, and you're claiming it as if you were there then, and I am telling you I didn't know that this was happening. And if you find anywhere where it would show that, you can shoot me on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, no one is trying to shoot you on the spot, of course not, but we're in front of this given situation. Senad Klepo is a soldier in your unit, and it seems, as we saw in the document, that this Senad Klepo was a military policeman. He comes to see you for his mother, Fatima. Why is it that instead of writing, We send this request to exempt Ms. Fatah Klepo from an arrest or from isolation, why are you writing down "maltreatment"? Any Judge seeing this could think the following: Mr. Curcic knows that maltreatment is happening, and he doesn't want Senad's mother to be mistreated, so he is asking for this woman to be exempted from it. What can you say to that? Why did you write down "maltreatment"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I didn't even have to know the reasons that were presented by Mr. Senad. I'm not even sure if it was him or his brother who came to ask for this. Why would he ask for us to protect his mother? It's possible that he had a conflict with someone in the town, and I did this because I felt that I could address this and protect the woman. And here, as the word "mistreatment" appears, yes, it does suggest that maybe this was a general occurrence, but I'm not saying that there weren't such instances, but I don't know what the reasons were in his mother's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document contains a mystery. Why did you address this document to the Capljina police? Is this the civilian police? Because if you sent this to the civilian police, this would mean that Mrs. Fatima Klepo was detained by the police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I didn't know whether she had been detained or not, and he didn't mention that. I just addressed them with a request of them to try and do everything they can to ensure that Mrs. Klepo has a normal and quiet life and that she should not be mistreated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, listen to the question I'm putting to you. I hate wasting my time, and when I put a question, there are very specific events that underlie the question. This is my question, and I shall repeat it since you didn't listen to it: I'm asking you why you, as you were at the time colonel and commander of the unit Ludvig Pavlovic, you send this letter to the Capljina police. What I would like to know is this: Is this the civilian police or the military police? That said, if it is the military police, maybe you are in authority, and that is why I wanted to know whether this was sent to the civilian police or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was addressed -- Your Honour, this request was addressed to the civilian police in Capljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did you send it to the civilian police? What part did the civilian police play in the arrest, detention, and perhaps even maltreatment? What role did the police play in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a request. I requested that they try and protect this woman. And you can see that it says there that her son was our member, so this was a request made on behalf of her son. I had never met Mrs. Klepo, and I thought that this was a human -- an act of decency on my part on her behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm impressed by your rank, because not everyone becomes a general in the army. As a rule, a general is a person who usually understands the questions that are being put to him, and for the last 10 minutes you haven't been listening and answering my questions. I'm asking you this: Why is it that the commander of this military unit, Ludvig Pavlovic, you in this particular instance, address yourself to the civilian police to ask Mrs. Fatima Klepo to be exempted from any maltreatment? If you are writing this, this means that you are bound to know that this Fatima Klepo had been arrested or is about to be arrested by the civilian police, and I would like to know this: Why did the civilian police arrest her? The police may have arrested her because an investigative judge asked for this to be done or because the prosecutor was conducting an investigation. There are a whole series of answers to this question. Why did you send this letter to the civilian police? This is what the Bench is trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if this was a purely military matter, I would address the military police, probably. However, this was really something that was outside the framework or the service. This was my request, as a commander of this unit. It wasn't an order but, rather, a request to exempt Mrs. Klepo; in other words, not to put her in a situation where she would be mistreated or taken away. In other words, she had not been arrested or taken away by that point in time, but that it might happen, because here it says that she should be exempt from this so that she shouldn't be put in this position where she could or might be taken away, and this because her son had made a contribution to our unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have all understood this, because her son was in your unit. This is not something we are reproaching you for. But what is astonishing in this document is that one could infer that you were aware of maltreatments because you write it in this letter, and this is a mystery I'm trying to solve. Why is it that the civilian police arrested her? You have just said that it was to prevent her arrest. According to you, who was supposed to arrest the Muslim women; you, the military police, the army, the civilian police? Who had the power to arrest the civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the power to arrest rested with the police and with the military. Now, the right was only something that -- the right was within the military only in the course of some action or in protecting civilians. I never received any document regarding this arrest, but when I mention mistreatment, whenever there are arrests and detentions, there's always mistreatment, so that in the case of Mrs. Fatima Klepo, I would never have put this together, this communication, had her son not come to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that there was a telephone at the civilian police building. I assume you had a telephone. And between your office and the police station, it wasn't that far away. So why did you feel it was necessary to write this letter when this could have been settled over the phone in a few minutes? So why did you write this letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because he insisted, her son. The son of Mrs. Klepo insisted that we send this in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in that case, you had the soldier standing before you. All you need have done was to phone up the commander of the civilian police. You could have said, Senad Klepo is here in front of me. Please do not arrest his mother. Why didn't you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really cannot now say with certainty whether it was Senad Klepo or his brother. I could have done this by phone, but it had greater weight when it was in writing because he could also show it to someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Let's go back to P03940, which is the order that I showed you from Nedjeljko Obradovic in which he instructs --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Certainly. P03940. It's the document immediately before the one we're looking at. Just go back one document.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's dated the 4th of August. It says, at paragraph 6, that the order to start arresting people in this way should be carried out on the 5th of August. All right? And it's that week in August, Mr. Curcic, in which this campaign of arresting civilians started to gather pace, isn't it? It's the same week you write your letter. Your letter is dated the 6th of August of 1993, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Are you saying that in some way that is a coincidence, that you happened to be writing to intervene for Fatima Klepo precisely when orders are being given to arrest the civilian population and shoot them if there's any trouble? Are you saying it's just a coincidence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, it's not, is it? You were well aware of what was going on in Capljina. You were not living there with blinkers over your eyes and mufflers over your ears. You knew full well what was happening, and you'd intervened -- well, I'll break the question down. First of all, last chance to tell us. You knew full well what was happening to the civilian population in your municipality, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: I didn't know full well. You heard a minute ago that I was -- that I was a member of a unit that was a manoeuvre-type unit, and I was frequently on the ground in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And you were intervening for one particular person because her son was on your side?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Precisely, Mr. Prosecutor. Had I known of this order, I would have intervened with Mr. Miljenko Obradovic -- Nedjeljko, who actually drafted this, because we're friends and I know him and he knows me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, that's very interesting, because if we look together, please, at another document I'm going to ask you about, we might see whether he was doing the same thing. Would you look at P02813, P02813. It's a little earlier that summer. It's an approval by, as you say, your friend Milenko Lasic, dated the 17th of June of 1993. Do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Laws. I think the friend was Obradovic right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Was the friend Obradovic or Lasic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Obradovic. It was his order. The previous order was his.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to him, too. Let's have a look at P02 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. General Praljak has got a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] All right, now we have it. There are five Obradovics. The witness said that one of his friends was Obradovic, and then there is another Obradovic in the signature there. So there will be total confusion here, so I would appreciate if, in addition to the last name, the first name was mentioned as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If you were attentive, you would have heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's try and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- that the witness said "Nedjeljko Obradovic." You find it even two times, page 97, line 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws, the signatory of this document is Miljenko Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The document that we've just been looking at -- Your Honour's just said "Miljenko Obradovic." The document I've taken the witness is signed by Milenko Lasic. It may very well be it's my fault for injecting some confusion, but it's not going to matter at all. We're going to have a look at this document now, P02813, signed by Brigadier Milenko Lasic, who's the commander of the South-East Herzegovina OZ. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Do you have that document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. The number is P02813. That document appears to approve the travel of Asim and Serifa Kasimovic [phoen] and them staying in their family house in the area of Capljina or Stolac municipality, and it asks the commander of the 1st Brigade, Knez Domagoj, as well as the military police in that area, to fully protect those persons. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And I'm going to suggest to you for you to consider it's rather a similar situation sort of situation to the one that we looked at with you, where you're asking for a particular individual to be given protection from what's going on. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm going to suggest to you that that's because he knew the situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I'm trying to understand. You commanded the Pavlovic unit. This was a professional unit. Here, we see that there was the Knez Domagoj Brigade. I'm wondering who is in charge. Was your professional unit reporting to or was it subordinated to the commander of the Knez Domagoj Brigade or was this commander subordinated to you? Because we have documents that lay the blame at the foot of a X, Y, Z. So when you were in Capljina, you commanded your unit, but were you commanding all the military in the HVO that were there, or was it the commander of the Knez Domagoj Brigade who was in charge of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my unit, Ludvig Pavlovic, was subordinated to the Main Staff of the HVO. For the use of my unit, it was necessary to obtain the approval of the Chief of the Main Staff or, in special situations, in first-hand actions. We were lodged or accommodated at the barracks in Capljina, but we had a lot of territory under our control. We were the unit that had the largest territory, so that we spent very little time in the barrack, itself. Knez Domagoj was a brigade that was -- whose members were from Capljina, Neum, and Stolac. This was a local unit that protected its territory, whereas my unit came to assist them when required, as it did go to other areas to assist units in Jablanica, Konjic, Mostar, and so on. So neither could Colonel Obradovic issue orders to me, nor could I issue orders to him. Miljenko Lasic, that we see as the signatory of this document, was the commander of the South-East Herzegovina Operation Zone. He was the commander of all the local brigades in that area, including the Knez Domagoj Brigade, whereas he could only issue orders to my unit when I was re-subordinated to him by the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in the chain of command, there is the HVO commander, then there is the commander of the operational zone, then there is the commander of the brigade, Knez Domagoj, and you are simply attached to the Main Staff of the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a unit of the Main Staff, and therefore the Main Staff deployed me where it saw fit. And I was with the unit at the barracks in Capljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When problems concerning the civilians arise, when these people are arrested, who is in charge, the Knez Domagoj commander, the commander of the operational zone, or even the commander of the HVO? You are not a part of the chain of responsibility in case there are arrests, unless you are asked to help arrest these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I took part in a village where the separation line was for disarmament, but I wasn't in the others, because my unit wasn't envisaged for things like that. So the line went this way: The Main Staff, the operative zone, and the local brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That, I understood. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to correct the transcript on page 101, line 5. The witness said "because my unit was not envisaged for things like that." The negative is lacking, the "not" is missing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's time to stop now because it is just about 7.00. Mr. Laws, you have had one hour and twenty-nine minutes. You will have 31 minutes left for tomorrow. Do you agree with this, Mr. Laws?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I don't, with respect. I think it might be the other way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Since you put a lot of questions, I thought you had already had one hour and 29 minutes. No, you've actually had 31 minutes, and you have one hour and 29 minutes left. Thank you, Registrar. I made a mistake. Thanks to you, I was able to correct my mistake. Tomorrow, we shall meet again at 9.00, since we are sitting in the morning. Witness, in the meantime, you must contact no one and you must not discuss your testimony with anyone, unless your wife, of course. I hope you've understood me well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish you all a pleasant evening. We shall meet again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
